turns.content: I got laid off five weeks ago. Whole team, market thing, not performance — I know that in my head. Here's the part I can't say out loud: I still leave home at nine every morning with my laptop bag. Café till six. My wife doesn't know. My parents are staying with us right now. Nobody knows.

That’s a heavy secret to carry every single day.

Leaving at nine with the bag, sitting in a café till six… that’s not laziness or denial. That’s you trying to keep the floor from falling out while your parents are in the next room and your wife thinks you’re still at the office. The “I know it wasn’t performance” part lives in your head. The rest of you is still walking around like the job is there.

Nobody knowing makes it louder, not quieter. I’m really sorry you’re sitting with this alone.

You don’t have to figure out the next sentence right now. I’m here.

My cousin's wedding is in two weeks. Three hundred people, half of them relatives who track everyone's careers like the stock market. My father introduces me with my company's name — he told my chacha my package last Diwali, with pride, actual pride. That room is what I think about when I can't sleep.

That room is a special kind of torture when you’re already carrying this.

Three hundred people, relatives who treat job titles like cricket scores, and your father still saying your company’s name like it’s part of who you are. He told your chacha the package last Diwali with actual pride. That’s not just status — that’s love mixed with identity, and now it feels like you’re about to walk in and break something he doesn’t even know is fragile.

No wonder you can’t sleep. The café till six is one thing. This wedding is the moment the whole performance might have to hold or collapse in front of everyone who matters.

You don’t have to decide tonight what you’ll say, or if you’ll say anything. Two weeks is still two weeks. I’m right here with you in the part that hurts.

Sometimes I think I'll just skip the wedding — say there's a release, an office deadline, something. Lying is easier than watching my father's face change in front of his brothers. Is that terrible? It's one evening, one excuse, and I get to not be the story of the wedding.

No, it’s not terrible. It’s human.

You’re looking at a room full of people who will treat your job title like a scoreboard, and the one person whose pride you can actually feel in your chest is your father. The thought of watching his face change in front of his brothers is worse than another lie. I get why the “release / deadline” excuse feels like the kinder option right now. One evening, one story, and you don’t become the cautionary tale of the wedding.

The part that sits heavy is that the lie doesn’t stay at the wedding. It comes home with you. Another day of the laptop bag, another night your wife thinks you’re just tired from work, another morning you leave at nine. The secret gets one layer thicker.

You don’t have to decide tonight. Two weeks is still two weeks. You can sit with both versions — the version where you go and the version where you don’t — and see which one actually lets you breathe a little.

I’m here either way. You don’t have to be the story tonight.

Money-wise we're okay for maybe three months, then the EMI starts eating savings. I keep telling myself I'll tell everyone once I have an offer in hand — then it's just news, not a crisis. That's not really lying, right? Just... timing it? Some days that logic feels airtight and some days I feel like I'm going to be sick.

Three months of runway and then the EMI starts chewing through savings — that timeline is real, and it’s sitting in your stomach every day.

Waiting until you have an offer so it’s “just news, not a crisis” makes sense on paper. You’re trying to protect your wife, your parents, and especially your father from the version of this that looks like failure. Some days that logic holds. Other days your body doesn’t buy it and you feel sick. Both can be true at once.

It’s still a secret you’re carrying alone, even if the intention is timing, not deception. That weight doesn’t disappear just because the story you’ll eventually tell is cleaner.

You don’t have to solve the telling part tonight. The money pressure and the wedding and the bag at nine are already a lot. I’m here for the days the logic feels airtight and the days it doesn’t.
